questions.q: Per this lesson's checklist, what should determine whether an integration uses the JWT Bearer/Client Credentials flows versus Authorization Code flow?
options: Whichever flow is fastest to configure in the connected app screen
The size of the org's data volume

Whether an individual human must explicitly consent -- unattended service-to-service integrations fit JWT Bearer/Client Credentials, while Authorization Code is reserved for cases needing individual human consent
Whether the integration uses REST or SOAP
questions.explain: This checklist item carries forward Lesson 2's reasoning: the deciding factor is whether a specific human needs to consent, not convenience or API style.

questions.q: According to this lesson's credential-storage checklist, when is a Protected Custom Metadata Type an acceptable place to store a secret?
options: Always, in any org configuration
Only genuinely inside a managed package -- otherwise it behaves like a plain custom setting and offers no real protection
Only when combined with API Only on the integration user's profile
Never, under any circumstances whatsoever
questions.explain: This directly carries forward Lesson 7's core caveat: Protected Custom Metadata only actually protects a secret inside a managed package context, which the checklist explicitly calls out as the exception rather than the default case.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is the difference between applying the checklist at 'design time' versus 'review time'?
options: They are two entirely different checklists with no overlap

The checklist itself doesn't change -- at design time it guides how to build correctly the first time, and at review time it becomes a set of verification questions checking for drift in something already running
Review-time checks are optional once an integration passes its initial design-time review
Design-time checks only apply to inbound integrations, review-time checks only to outbound
questions.explain: The same checklist serves both purposes -- the only difference is whether you're using it to build something correctly up front or to catch drift in something that's already live, which is exactly why Lesson 10 frames review as recurring, not one-time.

questions.q: When a review turns up multiple gaps at once, what does this lesson say should generally be prioritized first?
options: Documentation updates, since they take the least time
Network and monitoring improvements, since they're the easiest to implement

Identity and credential-storage gaps (a hardcoded, over-privileged, unrotated credential), and any exposed, unverified inbound endpoint -- since these carry the largest blast radius or are actively exploitable
Whichever gap was discovered first during the review, in chronological order
questions.explain: The lesson's default ordering (drawn from Lesson 11's case study) puts the largest-blast-radius and actively-exploitable gaps first -- identity/credential issues and unverified public endpoints -- with network and monitoring improvements as valuable but rarely the single most urgent fix.

questions.q: This lesson summarizes the entire course as answering four underlying questions. Which of the following is one of them?
options: How many Apex triggers does this integration's code use?
Is this integration built using Lightning Web Components?
What color scheme does the Salesforce UI use for this integration's Setup pages?
Would anyone notice if something went wrong with this integration?
questions.explain: The four underlying questions from Lesson 1, restated here, are: who/what is really making the call, is the credential safe at rest, can the network path and endpoint be trusted, and would anyone notice if something went wrong -- the last of these is exactly what monitoring and review (Lessons 9-10) exist to answer.
